newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Mexico slaps tariffs on U.S. corn syrup.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mexico slaps tariffs on U.S. corn syrup.

text.p: Mexico slapped import tariffs on high fructose corn syrup (HFCS) from the United States on Tuesday, moving to protect the national sugar industry from an invasion of the alternative sweetner.

The move, to be ratified Wednesday in the government's Official Gazette, follows an investigation against 17 major firms for "disloyal trade practices and dumping" of HFCS at prices below production cost.
Most of the biggest names of the world sugar and sweetner industry have been embroiled in the dumping allegations.

They include U.S. commodity giant Cargill Inc, British-based sugar conglomerate Tate & Lyle Plc, specialist corn syrup producer CPC International Inc and Archer Daniels Midland (ADM), the largest U.S. agricultural processing firm.

Mexico's National Sugar Chamber, the umbrella organisation for the country's mill owners, has long pushed the government to act to protect domestic sugar markets from the threat of being brushed aside by the corn-based sweetner, which is widely used in the soft drinks and food industries.

The government agreed February 27 to investigate the dumping allegations. The Trade Ministry announced Tuesday that it decided to impose provisional tariffs on HFCS imports and continue investigating until a final resolution can be made.
Tariffs of between $66.50 and $125.30 per tonne will be imposed on grade 42 HFCS (42 percent fructose) and between $63.40 and $175.50 per tonne of grade 55 HFCS (55 percent fructose), it added.
"These tariffs are equivalent to an average dumping margin of 102.2 percent for grade 42 syrup and 61.1 percent for grade 55 fructose," the ministry said in a statement.
It did not say when the provisional tariffs would be applied to the alternative sweetner, although edicts in the Official Gazette are normally applicable from the date of publication.
Francisco Sanchez, media spokesman for the National Sugar Chamber, said the Trade Ministry decision showed a willingness to support the national sugar industry.
"In principle it is good news, but it is provisional and it is not going to stop corn syrup from being imported but imports will be on a more level playing field," he added.
Mexican sugar industrialists have argued that U.S. farming subsidies allow corn syrup industries to produce the sweetner at unfair price advantages.
Carlos Artolozaga, a mill owner, told Reuters recently that the dumping allegations involved around 300,000 tonnes imported from the United States in 1996, mainly grade 55 (class 55) HFCSs.
Mexico imported around 350,000 tonnes of HFCS in 1996 and imports were expected to rise to 500,000 tonnes this year.
Mexico's soft drinks industry consumes around 1.5 million tonnes of the average national sugar harvest of 4.5 million tonnes.
